can_ip_forward.description: Whether to allow sending and receiving of packets with non-matching source or destination IPs. This defaults to false.
can_ip_forward.rationale: Allows instances to send or receive packets whose source or destination IP does not match the instance. This can enable routing or packet-forwarding behaviour, so a generic policy can require it to remain false unless explicitly approved.

deletion_policy.description:
Whether Terraform will be prevented from destroying the instance. Defaults to "DELETE".
When a 'terraform destroy' or 'terraform apply' would delete the instance,
the command will fail if this field is set to "PREVENT" in Terraform state.
When set to "ABANDON", the command will remove the resource from Terraform
management without updating or deleting the resource in the API.
When set to "DELETE", deleting the resource is allowed.
deletion_policy.rationale: Controls whether Terraform can perform destructive deletion of the resource. A platform policy can enforce a generic destroy-blocking value to prevent unintended destructive changes without assuming a specific environment tier.

description.description: A brief description of this resource.
description.rationale: Human-readable resource metadata only; it does not directly alter access, encryption, network exposure, or another security control.

instance_description.rationale: Human-readable descriptive metadata for instantiated VMs only; it does not directly alter access, encryption, network exposure, or another security control.

key_revocation_action_type.description: Action to be taken when a customer's encryption key is revoked. Supports "STOP" and "NONE", with "NONE" being the default.
key_revocation_action_type.rationale: Controls how the VM reacts when a customer-managed encryption key is revoked. Requiring STOP provides an enforceable response to key revocation instead of allowing the instance to continue operating with NONE.

labels.description:
A set of key/value label pairs to assign to instances created from this template,

				**Note**: This field is non-authoritative, and will only manage the labels present in your configuration.
				Please refer to the field 'effective_labels' for all of the labels present on the resource.
labels.rationale: Labels are cosmetic and organisational metadata. Required keys and values are organisation-specific, so they are not a generic security policy target.

machine_type.description: The machine type to create. To create a machine with a custom type (such as extended memory), format the value like custom-VCPUS-MEM_IN_MB like custom-6-20480 for 6 vCPU and 20GB of RAM.
machine_type.rationale: Selects compute capacity and hardware sizing. It is primarily a performance and cost choice rather than a generic security control.

metadata.description: Metadata key/value pairs to make available from within instances created from this template.
metadata.rationale: Free-form instance metadata can contain plaintext secrets, credentials, tokens, or other sensitive values. A platform policy can restrict unsafe metadata usage to reduce credential exposure and improve credential hygiene.

metadata_startup_script.description: An alternative to using the startup-script metadata key, mostly to match the compute_instance resource. This replaces the startup-script metadata key on the created instance and thus the two mechanisms are not allowed to be used simultaneously.
metadata_startup_script.rationale: Startup scripts execute commands when instances initialise and can embed secrets or run unverified commands. A platform policy can restrict inline startup scripts to reduce script-injection and credential-exposure risks.

min_cpu_platform.description: Specifies a minimum CPU platform. Applicable values are the friendly names of CPU platforms, such as Intel Haswell or Intel Skylake.
min_cpu_platform.rationale: Selects a minimum processor platform for compatibility or performance. It is not itself an access or protection control.

name.description: The name of the instance template. If you leave this blank, Terraform will auto-generate a unique name.
name.rationale: Identifies the template. Naming does not directly change permissions, exposure, encryption, or other security behaviour.

name_prefix.description: Creates a unique name beginning with the specified prefix. Conflicts with name.
name_prefix.rationale: Controls resource naming only. It does not directly affect security behaviour.

project.description: The ID of the project in which the resource belongs. If it is not provided, the provider project is used.
project.rationale: Identifies the owning project. Approved project IDs are organisation-specific references and should not be hardcoded by a generic platform policy.

region.description: The region in which the instance template is located. If it is not provided, the provider region is used.
region.rationale: Determines the region/zone where the resource is created. Policy should restrict it to an approved-region whitelist for data residency; the allowed set is parameterised (a hardcoded example whitelist is acceptable).

resource_manager_tags.description:
A map of resource manager tags.
				Resource manager tag keys and values have the same definition as resource manager tags. Keys must be in the format tagKeys/{tag_key_id}, and values are in the format tagValues/456. The field is ignored (both PUT & PATCH) when empty.
resource_manager_tags.rationale: Resource Manager tags can support attribute-based access control and security baselines. A platform policy can require mandatory security tags to be present without hardcoding organisation-specific tag values.

resource_policies.description: A list of self_links of resource policies to attach to the instance. Currently a max of 1 resource policy is supported.
resource_policies.rationale: References other resource-policy objects. Which policy resource is appropriate is organisation- and workload-specific, so specific identifiers should not be pinned generically.

tags.description: Tags to attach to the instance.
tags.rationale: Instance network tags can act as firewall targets. Unconstrained or overly broad tags can expose instances to unintended traffic or bypass security boundaries, so a platform policy can restrict their use.

advanced_machine_features.description: Controls for advanced machine-related behavior features.

advanced_machine_features.enable_nested_.description: Whether to enable nested virtualization or not.
advanced_machine_features.enable_nested_.rationale: Nested virtualization runs a hypervisor inside the VM and increases attack surface and potential privilege-escalation paths. A platform policy can require it to remain disabled by default unless explicitly necessary.

advanced_machine_features.enable_uefi_ne.description: Whether to enable UEFI networking or not.
advanced_machine_features.enable_uefi_ne.rationale: Controls UEFI networking capability for boot/runtime compatibility. It is not a generic access-control or protection setting.

advanced_machine_features.performance_mo.description: The PMU is a hardware component within the CPU core that monitors how the processor runs code. Valid values for the level of PMU are "STANDARD", "ENHANCED", and "ARCHITECTURAL".
advanced_machine_features.performance_mo.rationale: Controls performance-monitoring hardware exposure and capability. The appropriate level is workload-specific rather than a universal security requirement.

advanced_machine_features.threads_per_co.description: The number of threads per physical core. To disable simultaneous multithreading (SMT) set this to 1. If unset, the maximum number of threads supported per core by the underlying processor is assumed.
advanced_machine_features.threads_per_co.rationale: Controls CPU threading and performance characteristics. It is an operational tuning choice rather than a generic security control.

advanced_machine_features.turbo_mode.description: Turbo frequency mode to use for the instance. Currently supported modes is "ALL_CORE_MAX".
advanced_machine_features.turbo_mode.rationale: Controls CPU turbo behaviour for performance. It does not directly enforce a security boundary.

advanced_machine_features.visible_core_c.description: The number of physical cores to expose to an instance. Multiply by the number of threads per core to compute the total number of virtual CPUs to expose to the instance. If unset, the number of cores is inferred from the instance\'s nominal CPU count and the underlying platform\'s SMT width.
advanced_machine_features.visible_core_c.rationale: Controls the amount of CPU capacity exposed to the VM. It is a sizing/performance setting rather than a security control.

confidential_instance_config.description: The Confidential VM config being used by the instance. on_host_maintenance has to be set to TERMINATE or this will fail to create.

confidential_instance_config.confidentia.description:
The confidential computing technology the instance uses.
								SEV is an AMD feature. TDX is an Intel feature. One of the following
								values is required: SEV, SEV_SNP, TDX. If SEV_SNP, min_cpu_platform =
								"AMD Milan" is currently required.
confidential_instance_config.confidentia.rationale: Chooses among supported confidential-computing technologies. The security control is whether confidential compute is enabled; the specific technology is a compatibility and workload choice.

confidential_instance_config.enable_conf.description: Defines whether the instance should have confidential compute enabled. Field will be deprecated in a future release.
confidential_instance_config.enable_conf.rationale: Enables Confidential VM protections that encrypt data while it is being processed. This is an explicit security feature that can be centrally required for workloads that need confidential computing.

disk.description: Disks to attach to instances created from this template. This can be specified multiple times for multiple disks.

disk.architecture.description: The architecture of the image. Allowed values are ARM64 or X86_64.
disk.architecture.rationale: Selects disk/image CPU architecture compatibility. It is not a security control.

disk.auto_delete.description: Whether or not the disk should be auto-deleted. This defaults to true.
disk.auto_delete.rationale: Controls disk lifecycle when the instance is deleted. Retention and cleanup are operational data-management choices, distinct from destructive-resource protection.

disk.boot.description: Indicates that this is a boot disk.
disk.boot.rationale: Marks a disk as the boot disk. This is a functional configuration choice rather than a generic security control.

disk.device_name.description: A unique device name that is reflected into the /dev/ tree of a Linux operating system running within the instance. If not specified, the server chooses a default device name to apply to this disk.
disk.device_name.rationale: Defines the guest-visible device identifier. It does not directly alter permissions or data protection.

disk.disk_name.description: Name of the disk. When not provided, this defaults to the name of the instance.
disk.disk_name.rationale: Names the disk. Resource naming is not itself a security control.

disk.disk_size_gb.description: The size of the image in gigabytes. If not specified, it will inherit the size of its base image. For SCRATCH disks, the size must be one of 375 or 3000 GB, with a default of 375 GB.
disk.disk_size_gb.rationale: Controls storage capacity. It is a cost and capacity setting rather than a security control.

disk.disk_type.description: The Google Compute Engine disk type. Such as "pd-ssd", "local-ssd", "pd-balanced" or "pd-standard".
disk.disk_type.rationale: Selects the storage performance class. It is primarily a performance/cost decision.

disk.guest_os_features.description: A list of features to enable on the guest operating system. Applicable only for bootable images.
disk.guest_os_features.rationale: Guest OS features affect platform compatibility and security boundaries. Enabling unsupported or legacy features can weaken isolation or introduce unsafe guest-host interactions, so a platform policy can constrain them.

disk.interface.description: Specifies the disk interface to use for attaching this disk.
disk.interface.rationale: The disk interface type affects the VM's storage driver path and virtualization isolation architecture. A platform policy can restrict interface choices to approved secure options rather than treating the setting only as performance tuning.

disk.labels.description: A set of key/value label pairs to assign to disks,
disk.labels.rationale: Disk labels are commonly used for data classification, compliance tracking, and security asset inventory. A platform policy can require appropriate label presence without hardcoding organisation-specific values.

disk.mode.description: The mode in which to attach this disk, either READ_WRITE or READ_ONLY. If you are attaching or creating a boot disk, this must read-write mode.
disk.mode.rationale: Disk attachment mode controls whether a volume is writable. Requiring read-only mode for applicable non-boot data disks can reduce unauthorized modification, tampering, and malware persistence.

disk.provisioned_iops.description: Indicates how many IOPS to provision for the disk. This sets the number of I/O operations per second that the disk can handle. For more details, see the [Extreme persistent disk documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/extreme-persistent-disk) or the [Hyperdisk documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/hyperdisks) depending on the selected disk_type.
disk.provisioned_iops.rationale: Provisioned IOPS controls disk performance capacity. Bounding IOPS can help prevent resource-exhaustion abuse, uncontrolled high-tier consumption, and operational instability, making it suitable for a platform guardrail.

disk.provisioned_throughput.description: Indicates how much throughput to provision for the disk, in MB/s. This sets the amount of data that can be read or written from the disk per second. Values must greater than or equal to 1. For more details, see the [Hyperdisk documentation](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/hyperdisks).
disk.provisioned_throughput.rationale: Provisioned throughput controls how quickly data can be read or written. Bounding throughput can limit runaway workloads, resource abuse, and excessive data-exfiltration capacity while supporting operational stability.

disk.resource_manager_tags.description: A map of resource manager tags. Resource manager tag keys and values have the same definition as resource manager tags. Keys must be in the format tagKeys/{tag_key_id}, and values are in the format tagValues/456. The field is ignored (both PUT & PATCH) when empty.
disk.resource_manager_tags.rationale: Disk Resource Manager tags can support data classification and compliance controls. A platform policy can require mandatory security-tag presence while leaving organisation-specific tag keys and values configurable.

disk.resource_policies.description: A list (short name or id) of resource policies to attach to this disk. Currently a max of 1 resource policy is supported.
disk.resource_policies.rationale: Attaching a resource policy can enforce data-protection controls such as backup or retention baselines. A platform policy can require that an appropriate resource policy is attached without pinning a specific policy identifier.

disk.source.description: The name (not self_link) of the disk (such as those managed by google_compute_disk) to attach. ~> Note: Either source or source_image is required when creating a new instance except for when creating a local SSD.
disk.source.rationale: References an existing disk. Which disk is trusted is organisation-specific and should not be hardcoded by a generic policy.

disk.source_image.description: The image from which to initialize this disk. This can be one of: the image's self_link, projects/{project}/global/images/{image}, projects/{project}/global/images/family/{family}, global/images/{image}, global/images/family/{family}, family/{family}, {project}/{family}, {project}/{image}, {family}, or {image}. ~> Note: Either source or source_image is required when creating a new instance except for when creating a local SSD.
disk.source_image.rationale: References an image used to create the disk. Approved image identifiers are organisation-specific references rather than a universal value policy.

disk.source_snapshot.description:
The source snapshot to create this disk. When creating
a new instance, one of initializeParams.sourceSnapshot,
initializeParams.sourceImage, or disks.source is
required except for local SSD.
disk.source_snapshot.rationale: References a snapshot used to create the disk. Approved snapshot identifiers are organisation-specific.

disk.storage_pool.description: The self_link or ID of the Storage Pool to create this disk in.
disk.storage_pool.rationale: References a storage-pool resource. The valid pool is an environment-specific resource reference.

disk.type.description: The type of Google Compute Engine disk, can be either "SCRATCH" or "PERSISTENT".
disk.type.rationale: Selects SCRATCH or PERSISTENT storage based on workload requirements. It is primarily an operational storage-lifecycle choice.

disk.disk_encryption_key.description: Encrypts or decrypts a disk using a customer-supplied encryption key.

disk.disk_encryption_key.kms_key_self_li.description: The self link of the encryption key that is stored in Google Cloud KMS.
disk.disk_encryption_key.kms_key_self_li.rationale: Specifies the Cloud KMS key used for disk encryption. A platform policy can require this value to be set and non-blank to enforce customer-managed encryption while avoiding pinning any specific key identifier.

disk.disk_encryption_key.kms_key_service.description: The service account being used for the encryption request for the given KMS key. If absent, the Compute Engine default service account is used.
disk.disk_encryption_key.kms_key_service.rationale: Specifies the service account used for KMS encryption operations. A platform policy can require an explicit, non-default run-as service account to support least privilege without pinning a specific account.

disk.source_image_encryption_key.description:
The customer-supplied encryption key of the source
image. Required if the source image is protected by a
customer-supplied encryption key.

Instance templates do not store customer-supplied
encryption keys, so you cannot create disks for
instances in a managed instance group if the source
images are encrypted with your own keys.

disk.source_image_encryption_key.kms_key.description:
The self link of the encryption key that is stored in
Google Cloud KMS. Only one of kms_key_self_link, rsa_encrypted_key and raw_key may be set.
disk.source_image_encryption_key.kms_key.rationale: References the key required to decrypt an already-encrypted source image. It does not itself determine whether the resulting disk uses a secure encryption policy and the key identifier is environment-specific.

disk.source_image_encryption_key.kms_key.description:
The service account being used for the encryption
request for the given KMS key. If absent, the Compute
Engine default service account is used.
disk.source_image_encryption_key.kms_key.rationale: Specifies the run-as service account used for source-image KMS operations. A platform policy can require an explicit, non-default service account for least privilege without hardcoding a specific email address.

disk.source_image_encryption_key.raw_key.description: Specifies a 256-bit customer-supplied encryption key, encoded in RFC 4648 base64 to either encrypt or decrypt this resource.  Only one of kms_key_self_link, rsa_encrypted_key and raw_key may be set.
disk.source_image_encryption_key.raw_key.rationale: Places a raw customer-supplied encryption key in configuration. Raw key material is sensitive and can be exposed through configuration or state, so a policy can prohibit raw keys and prefer managed or wrapped key mechanisms.

disk.source_image_encryption_key.rsa_enc.description: Specifies an RFC 4648 base64 encoded, RSA-wrapped 2048-bit customer-supplied encryption key to either encrypt or decrypt this resource.  Only one of kms_key_self_link, rsa_encrypted_key and raw_key may be set.
disk.source_image_encryption_key.rsa_enc.rationale: Uses a statically wrapped customer-supplied encryption key for the source image. A platform policy can discourage customer-supplied wrapping keys in favour of platform-managed CMEK to reduce secret-handling risk.

disk.source_snapshot_encryption_key.description: The customer-supplied encryption key of the source snapshot.

disk.source_snapshot_encryption_key.kms_.description:
The self link of the encryption key that is stored in
Google Cloud KMS. Only one of kms_key_self_link, rsa_encrypted_key and raw_key may be set.
disk.source_snapshot_encryption_key.kms_.rationale: Specifies the Cloud KMS key used with the encrypted source snapshot. A platform policy can require a non-blank customer-managed key reference without pinning a specific key name.

disk.source_snapshot_encryption_key.kms_.description:
The service account being used for the encryption
request for the given KMS key. If absent, the Compute
Engine default service account is used.
disk.source_snapshot_encryption_key.kms_.rationale: Specifies the run-as service account used for source-snapshot KMS operations. A platform policy can require an explicit, non-default service account for least privilege without pinning a specific identity.

disk.source_snapshot_encryption_key.raw_.description: Specifies a 256-bit customer-supplied encryption key, encoded in RFC 4648 base64 to either encrypt or decrypt this resource. Only one of kms_key_self_link, rsa_encrypted_key and raw_key may be set.
disk.source_snapshot_encryption_key.raw_.rationale: Places a raw customer-supplied encryption key in configuration. Raw key material is sensitive and can be exposed through configuration or state, so a policy can prohibit raw keys and prefer managed or wrapped key mechanisms.

disk.source_snapshot_encryption_key.rsa_.description: Specifies an RFC 4648 base64 encoded, RSA-wrapped 2048-bit customer-supplied encryption key to either encrypt or decrypt this resource.  Only one of kms_key_self_link, rsa_encrypted_key and raw_key may be set.
disk.source_snapshot_encryption_key.rsa_.rationale: Uses a statically wrapped customer-supplied encryption key for the source snapshot. A platform policy can discourage customer-supplied wrapping keys in favour of platform-managed CMEK to reduce secret-handling risk.

guest_accelerator.description: List of the type and count of accelerator cards attached to the instance.

guest_accelerator.count.description: The number of the guest accelerator cards exposed to this instance.
guest_accelerator.count.rationale: Controls the quantity of accelerator hardware attached to instances. A platform policy can bound or whitelist high-privilege or costly accelerator tiers to prevent unintended GPU sprawl and unauthorized high-tier resource consumption.

guest_accelerator.type.description: The accelerator type resource to expose to this instance. E.g. nvidia-tesla-k80.
guest_accelerator.type.rationale: Selects accelerator hardware. It is a workload/performance choice rather than a generic security control.

network_interface.description: Networks to attach to instances created from this template. This can be specified multiple times for multiple networks.

network_interface.igmp_query.description: Indicates whether igmp query is enabled on the network interface or not. If enabled, also indicates the version of IGMP supported.
network_interface.igmp_query.rationale: Controls multicast/IGMP behaviour for specific networking use cases. Whether it is needed is network-design specific rather than universally insecure.

network_interface.network.description: The name or self_link of the network to attach this interface to. Use network attribute for Legacy or Auto subnetted networks and subnetwork for custom subnetted networks.
network_interface.network.rationale: References the VPC network to attach. Approved network names are organisation-specific resource references.

network_interface.network_attachment.description: The URL of the network attachment that this interface should connect to in the following format: projects/{projectNumber}/regions/{region_name}/networkAttachments/{network_attachment_name}.
network_interface.network_attachment.rationale: References a network attachment resource. The correct attachment is environment-specific and should not be hardcoded generically.

network_interface.network_ip.description: The private IP address to assign to the instance. If empty, the address will be automatically assigned.
network_interface.network_ip.rationale: Specifies a private IP address. Address selection is environment-specific and the value is not inherently insecure.

network_interface.nic_type.description: The type of vNIC to be used on this interface. Possible values:GVNIC, VIRTIO_NET, MRDMA, IRDMA and IDPF
network_interface.nic_type.rationale: Selects the virtual NIC implementation for compatibility and performance. It is not a generic security control.

network_interface.queue_count.description: The networking queue count that's specified by users for the network interface. Both Rx and Tx queues will be set to this number. It will be empty if not specified.
network_interface.queue_count.rationale: Controls networking queue capacity and performance. It is an operational tuning setting.

network_interface.stack_type.description: The stack type for this network interface to identify whether the IPv6 feature is enabled or not. If not specified, IPV4_ONLY will be used.
network_interface.stack_type.rationale: Selects IPv4-only or dual-stack capability. IPv6 support itself is not inherently insecure; external exposure is controlled separately.

network_interface.subnetwork.description: The name of the subnetwork to attach this interface to. The subnetwork must exist in the same region this instance will be created in. Either network or subnetwork must be provided.
network_interface.subnetwork.rationale: Controls which subnetwork the instance joins. Restricting deployment to approved, segment-aligned subnets is a core network-exposure control and helps maintain intended security boundaries.

network_interface.subnetwork_project.description: The ID of the project in which the subnetwork belongs. If it is not provided, the provider project is used.
network_interface.subnetwork_project.rationale: Controls the project from which the attached subnetwork is selected. A platform policy can restrict cross-project network attachment to approved boundaries and prevent unauthorized deployment into external projects.

network_interface.vlan.description: VLAN tag of a dynamic network interface, must be an integer in the range from 2 to 255 inclusively.
network_interface.vlan.rationale: Assigns a VLAN identifier to a dynamic network interface. A platform policy can restrict VLAN assignments to authorized segmentation boundaries to maintain workload isolation.

network_interface.access_config.description: Access configurations, i.e. IPs via which this instance can be accessed via the Internet. Omit to ensure that the instance is not accessible from the Internet (this means that ssh provisioners will not work unless you are running Terraform can send traffic to the instance's network (e.g. via tunnel or because it is running on another cloud instance on that network). This block can be repeated multiple times.

network_interface.access_config.nat_ip.description: The IP address that will be 1:1 mapped to the instance's network ip. If not given, one will be generated.
network_interface.access_config.nat_ip.rationale: Assigns an external IPv4 address to the instance through an access configuration, increasing Internet exposure. A policy can restrict or prohibit explicit public IP assignment.

network_interface.access_config.network_.description: The networking tier used for configuring this instance template. This field can take the following values: PREMIUM, STANDARD, FIXED_STANDARD. If this field is not specified, it is assumed to be PREMIUM.
network_interface.access_config.network_.rationale: Selects the network service tier for external access. Network tiers can affect routing paths and integration with security controls such as Cloud Armor, so a platform policy can enforce an approved secure tier.

network_interface.alias_ip_range.description: An array of alias IP ranges for this network interface. Can only be specified for network interfaces on subnet-mode networks.

network_interface.alias_ip_range.ip_cidr.description: The IP CIDR range represented by this alias IP range. This IP CIDR range must belong to the specified subnetwork and cannot contain IP addresses reserved by system or used by other network interfaces. At the time of writing only a netmask (e.g. /24) may be supplied, with a CIDR format resulting in an API error.
network_interface.alias_ip_range.ip_cidr.rationale: Defines an alias IP range for the interface. A platform policy can enforce valid approved internal address ranges to support IPAM governance and prevent address overlap or exhaustion.

network_interface.alias_ip_range.subnetw.description: The subnetwork secondary range name specifying the secondary range from which to allocate the IP CIDR range for this alias IP range. If left unspecified, the primary range of the subnetwork will be used.
network_interface.alias_ip_range.subnetw.rationale: Selects the subnet secondary range used for alias IP allocation. A platform policy can require approved secondary ranges so alias addresses map to intended internal segmentation structures.

network_interface.ipv6_access_config.description: An array of IPv6 access configurations for this interface. Currently, only one IPv6 access config, DIRECT_IPV6, is supported. If there is no ipv6AccessConfig specified, then this instance will have no external IPv6 Internet access.

network_interface.ipv6_access_config.net.description: The service-level to be provided for IPv6 traffic when the subnet has an external subnet. Only PREMIUM tier is valid for IPv6
network_interface.ipv6_access_config.net.rationale: This leaf exists inside an IPv6 access configuration that provides external IPv6 Internet access. A policy can reject this configuration where instances must remain privately addressed.

network_performance_config.description: Configures network performance settings for the instance. If not specified, the instance will be created with its default network performance configuration.

network_performance_config.total_egress_.description: The egress bandwidth tier to enable. Possible values:TIER_1, DEFAULT
network_performance_config.total_egress_.rationale: Controls network performance capacity. It is an operational/performance setting rather than a security control.

reservation_affinity.description: Specifies the reservations that this instance can consume from.

reservation_affinity.type.description: The type of reservation from which this instance can consume resources.
reservation_affinity.type.rationale: Controls how the VM consumes reservations. It is a capacity-placement choice rather than a security control.

reservation_affinity.specific_reservatio.description: Specifies the label selector for the reservation to use.

Corresponds to the label key of a reservation resource. To target a SPECIFIC_RESERVATION by name, specify compute.googleapis.com/reservation-name as the key and specify the name of your reservation as the only value.
reservation_affinity.specific_reservatio.rationale: Identifies a reservation selector key. The correct selector is organisation-specific metadata.

reservation_affinity.specific_reservatio.description: Corresponds to the label values of a reservation resource.
reservation_affinity.specific_reservatio.rationale: Identifies reservation selector values. The correct values are organisation-specific.

scheduling.automatic_restart.description: Specifies whether the instance should be automatically restarted if it is terminated by Compute Engine (not terminated by a user). This defaults to true.
scheduling.automatic_restart.rationale: Controls availability behaviour after infrastructure termination. It is an operational resilience choice rather than a security control.

scheduling.availability_domain.description: Specifies the availability domain, which this instance should be scheduled on.
scheduling.availability_domain.rationale: Controls placement for availability. It is an operational scheduling choice.

scheduling.instance_termination_action.description: Specifies the action GCE should take when SPOT VM is preempted.
scheduling.instance_termination_action.rationale: Controls what happens when a Spot VM is preempted. It is an operational lifecycle choice.

scheduling.on_host_maintenance.description: Defines the maintenance behavior for this instance.
scheduling.on_host_maintenance.rationale: Controls maintenance behaviour. The appropriate action depends on workload availability requirements rather than a universal security rule.

scheduling.preemptible.description: Allows instance to be preempted. This defaults to false.
scheduling.preemptible.rationale: Preemptible instances can be terminated and reclaimed abruptly, which can affect availability, integrity, and workload stability. A platform policy can prohibit preemptible instances for sensitive or production workloads.

scheduling.provisioning_model.description: Whether the instance is spot. If this is set as SPOT.
scheduling.provisioning_model.rationale: Spot or other non-standard provisioning models can be terminated unexpectedly and reduce workload stability. A platform policy can require standard provisioning for sensitive workloads to protect critical services from sudden termination.

scheduling.termination_time.description:
Specifies the timestamp, when the instance will be terminated,
in RFC3339 text format. If specified, the instance termination action
will be performed at the termination time.
scheduling.termination_time.rationale: An automatic termination time can prematurely stop security appliances, monitoring agents, or critical services. A platform policy can restrict time-bounded instances to prevent unintended loss of security controls and service integrity.

scheduling.local_ssd_recovery_timeout.description:
Specifies the maximum amount of time a Local Ssd Vm should wait while
  recovery of the Local Ssd state is attempted. Its value should be in
  between 0 and 168 hours with hour granularity and the default value being 1
  hour.

scheduling.local_ssd_recovery_timeout.na.description:
Span of time that's a fraction of a second at nanosecond
resolution. Durations less than one second are represented
with a 0 seconds field and a positive nanos field. Must
be from 0 to 999,999,999 inclusive.
scheduling.local_ssd_recovery_timeout.na.rationale: Controls Local SSD recovery timing after host failure. A platform policy can constrain recovery timeouts because inappropriate values can affect data availability, recovery integrity, and handling of persistent or encrypted state.

scheduling.local_ssd_recovery_timeout.se.description:
Span of time at a resolution of a second.
Must be from 0 to 315,576,000,000 inclusive.
scheduling.local_ssd_recovery_timeout.se.rationale: Controls Local SSD recovery timing after host failure. A platform policy can constrain recovery timeouts because they directly affect data availability, recovery integrity, and post-failure data handling.

scheduling.max_run_duration.description: The timeout for new network connections to hosts.

scheduling.max_run_duration.nanos.description:
Span of time that's a fraction of a second at nanosecond
resolution. Durations less than one second are represented
with a 0 seconds field and a positive nanos field. Must
be from 0 to 999,999,999 inclusive.
scheduling.max_run_duration.nanos.rationale: Controls the maximum lifetime of an instance. Enforcing bounded run duration can support ephemeral-compute practices so credentials and sessions do not persist indefinitely on long-running nodes.

scheduling.max_run_duration.seconds.description:
Span of time at a resolution of a second.
Must be from 0 to 315,576,000,000 inclusive.
scheduling.max_run_duration.seconds.rationale: Controls the maximum lifetime of an instance. Limiting run duration reduces the exposure window of compromised long-running nodes and supports credential hygiene, session lifecycle management, and ephemeral-compute practices.

scheduling.node_affinities.description: Specifies node affinities or anti-affinities to determine which sole-tenant nodes your instances and managed instance groups will use as host systems.

scheduling.node_affinities.key.description: Corresponds to the label key of a reservation resource. To target a SPECIFIC_RESERVATION by name, specify compute.googleapis.com/reservation-name as the key and specify the name of your reservation as the only value.
scheduling.node_affinities.key.rationale: Node-affinity selector keys are placement metadata and references specific to tenant isolation or hardware-allocation needs, making them unsuitable for a generic multi-tenant platform policy.

scheduling.node_affinities.operator.rationale: Controls how node-affinity placement constraints are evaluated. Restricting operators to approved forms can support workload isolation and secure placement for multi-tenant or sensitive workloads.

scheduling.node_affinities.values.description: Corresponds to the label values of a reservation resource.
scheduling.node_affinities.values.rationale: Node-affinity values restrict where instances can run and therefore form part of tenancy and isolation enforcement. A platform policy can require approved node-group constraints without hardcoding specific names.

service_account.description: Service account to attach to the instance.

service_account.email.description: The service account e-mail address. If not given, the default Google Compute Engine service account is used.
service_account.email.rationale: Controls the run-as service account attached to the instance. A platform policy can require an explicit, non-default service account to support least privilege while avoiding pinning a specific email address.

service_account.scopes.description: A list of service scopes. Both OAuth2 URLs and gcloud short names are supported. To allow full access to all Cloud APIs, use the cloud-platform scope.
service_account.scopes.rationale: OAuth scopes contribute to least-privilege access even though IAM roles provide primary authorization. A platform policy can reject overly broad or legacy all-access scopes, such as unrestricted cloud-platform access, and require a secure minimum scope shape.

shielded_instance_config.description: Enable Shielded VM on this instance. Shielded VM provides verifiable integrity to prevent against malware and rootkits. Defaults to disabled. Note: shielded_instance_config can only be used with boot images with shielded vm support.

shielded_instance_config.enable_integrit.description: Compare the most recent boot measurements to the integrity policy baseline and return a pair of pass/fail results depending on whether they match or not. Defaults to true.
shielded_instance_config.enable_integrit.rationale: Enables Shielded VM integrity monitoring so boot measurements can be checked against an integrity baseline. This is a direct VM-hardening control and can be required by policy.

shielded_instance_config.enable_secure_b.description: Verify the digital signature of all boot components, and halt the boot process if signature verification fails. Defaults to false.
shielded_instance_config.enable_secure_b.rationale: Enables Secure Boot, which verifies boot-component signatures and helps prevent untrusted boot software from loading. This is a direct security-hardening control.

shielded_instance_config.enable_vtpm.description: Use a virtualized trusted platform module, which is a specialized computer chip you can use to encrypt objects like keys and certificates. Defaults to true.
shielded_instance_config.enable_vtpm.rationale: Enables the virtual Trusted Platform Module used by Shielded VM for measured boot and protection of keys and integrity data. This is a direct security-hardening control.
